title: Request preparse / header-sieve sampler notes
content:
Context:
This is a working notebook of experiments and observations focused on the very first CPU work for small/short requests: the "preparse" stage I define as everything that happens before tokenization and model dispatch. That includes: TCP/HTTP framing, header parsing, auth checks, route selection, small JSON body parsing, and early routing decisions (which model/variant to use).

Motivation / hypothesis:
We keep seeing tail latency spikes on tiny requests (a single prompt, ~30 tokens) where the serving runtime's overall CPU is low but request latency has a heavy 99th percentile. Hypothesis: the small-request hot path is dominated by Python-side preparse work and the GIL/cpython parsing costs not visible in larger-batch profiling. If we can push the smallest bits of parsing off the main worker threads or make them C-native, we can reduce tail latency and free worker cycles for model-serving paths.

Experiment goals:
- Quantify how much time preparse (headers + json parse + route selection) takes on single-token/small requests.
- Capture where the main-thread stalls occur (GIL, IO wait, blocking system calls).
- Try two mitigations: (A) a tiny C extension that parses headers + extracts route key ("header-sieve"), and (B) a dedicated lightweight process pool for preparse (multiproc worker that returns a preparse token).

Environment and test harness:
- Runtime image: rwinf/serving-runtime:canary-2024-11 (py3.11, uvloop, CPython)
- Machines: c6a.large-equivalent (8 vCPU, 32GB) single-node dev cluster
- Load generator: custom Go harness that sends HTTP/1.1 requests with persistent connections, 2000 concurrent connections, target throughput 400 qps (to generate singles).
- Request shape: POST /v1/generate with header X-Model: redwood/llama-13b, body {"prompt":"short"} - body size 50–120 bytes.
- Tools: py-spy (flame and top), strace, perf top, pprof from C++ worker, and micro-bench harnessed timers.

Baseline measurements (no changes):
- P95 latency: 18.4 ms
- P99 latency: 92.7 ms
- Mean CPU per worker: 12%
- Observed that 60% of P99 events had >40ms spent entirely in Python preparse stack (py-spy samples show JSONDecoder and dict creation as hot)

Profiling notes (py-spy + flame):
- Top functions sampled: json.loads, http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler.parse_request (we use an async wrapper but still see CPython parse), jwt.decode (auth) for some tenants, route_lookup (Python dict + regex matching), and a lot of time in builtins: PyObject_Call, PyDict_SetItem.
- GIL contention: py-spy shows many threads stuck at _PyEval_EvalFrameDefault waiting, which correlates with CPU bursts on a single core.
- syscalls: strace showed read()/recv() bursts followed by immediate CPU work -- not IO wait-bound.

Mitigation A: header-sieve C extension (PoC)
- What: tiny C module that is built as a CPython extension; given a bytes buffer for the header + first N bytes of body, it scans for X-Model header, extracts value, and finds Content-Length boundary. Returns a small tuple (model_key, body_offset). It avoids json.loads for the very common shape where body is small and just {"prompt":"..."}.
- Rationale: header parsing and small pattern extraction is extremely cheap in C and avoids many PyObject allocations per request.
- Implementation details: borrowed fast HTTP header scanner from existing internal C util; minimal allocation; API is sieve.parse_first(bytes)-> (model, offset)
- Results:
  - P95: 14.1 ms (23% improvement)
  - P99: 45.5 ms (51% improvement)
  - mean CPU per worker: +1% (negligible)
  - Observations: py-spy shows json.loads time reduced by ~60% for small bodies because we replaced the initial extraction. Still need to call json.loads to get the actual prompt string, but often we can slice bytes and pass to tokenizer as bytes -> this avoids constructing intermediate python string in some codepaths.
- Downsides: C extension needs maintenance, adds build complexity, and is only useful for the most common request shapes. Not a total win for tenants with complex JSON bodies.

Mitigation B: preparse proc pool (multiprocess)
- What: spawn a small pool of 4 lightweight processes (uvloop main process keeps accepting sockets). For each request, we do an async handoff of the first 256 bytes to the pool over a unix socket; worker parses headers and small JSON and returns a struct. This isolates GIL/GIL-related allocation from main worker threads.
- Rationale: using processes avoids single-threaded GIL stalls affecting main event loop. We can keep pool size small and reuse processes.
- Results:
  - P95: 13.7 ms
  - P99: 38.6 ms (best P99 observed)
  - mean CPU per worker: worker CPU decreased (parsing work moved to pool) but total system CPU increased ~8% due to process overhead.
  - Observations: much cleaner py-spy stacks on main; however context-switch and serialization overhead matters. The pool is only worth it when preparse time > 8ms on average.
- Downsides: IPC complexity, failure modes (process death), backpressure when pool overloaded, harder to autoscale per-tenant.

Other small experiments:
- ujson / orjson: swapping json.loads for orjson.loads reduced average preparse time by ~30% but didn't eliminate allocations. P99 improvement ~20%. Good as low-effort change.
- Reusing dicts via object pools: attempted micro-allocator trick to reuse request-scoped dicts. Complexity high and win small (~5%). Not recommended.
- Move JWT verification to C library (pyjwt with C backend): marginal improvement when auth is active (10–15% on preparse). Worth doing if many tenants use JWT.

End-to-end observations and recommendations:
1) For small-request tail latency, the biggest wins are (in order): move preparse off the main worker (proc pool), replace Python header/body extraction with C-level parsing, and swap to orjson. Combine these for additive improvements.
2) PoC showed the preparse step accounts for ~35–70% of P99 latency for tiny requests. Fixing it yields outsized P99 reductions even if overall CPU is low.
3) Implementation tradeoffs: C extension has lower operational complexity but narrower applicability; proc-pool is more general but requires robust lifecycle management.
4) Quick wins: enable orjson where safe (feature-flag per-route), add a lightweight path that returns a tokenized payload for repeated small prompts (pre-tokenize cache keyed by body fingerprint).
5) Long-term: evaluate moving HTTP framing & routing into a small Rust/NIF component (see linked RFC). Could be folded into the edge proxy, but we want runtime-local minimal parsing to avoid cross-service hop.

Open questions / next steps:
- What is expected tenant distribution for complex vs simple JSON shapes? Need sampling across production traffic.
- Failure modes for the preprocess pool: how to fail back to Python path gracefully without big latency cliffs?
- Security review for C extension. Edge cases around malformed headers.
- Autoscaling strategy: if preparse is offloaded, how should worker pool sizing be adjusted?

Immediate action items:
- (Aisha) Stabilize orjson rollout patch behind feature flag (PR: linked). Target: canary next week.
- (Markus) Flesh out the proc-pool supervisor (minimal heartbeat + restart) and a benchmark harness that simulates pool saturation.
- (Diego) Prototype a smaller Rust header parser as a library (pooled via cbindgen) to compare with CPython C extension.

Appendix: micro commands (how we measured)
- py-spy record --native -o flame.svg -- python -m serving.runtime.main (sample rate 1000Hz)
- go-hammerer --connections=2000 --qps=400 --path=/v1/generate --header="X-Model:redwood/13b" --body='{"prompt":"short"}'
- strace -f -p <pid> -e trace=network,read,write -s 256

Notes to self: prioritize orjson + keep PoC C extension in tree for quick compile; proc-pool is promising but needs more chaos testing.
